data.content_ref: inline:The target claims the dilemma 'dissolves' and that 'the underlying structure was never relevant to the outcome at all,' yet its own counterconditions concede the three most common situations in which the dilemma re-asserts itself. The 'Eliminative Default' mechanism only produces a unique action-guiding outcome when exactly one theory remains unrefuted; when multiple unrefuted theories coexist (countercondition 1), or when acting on a false-but-unrefuted theory carries differential costs requiring a probability estimate (countercondition 2), the agent still needs a basis for choosing among survivors. These are not exotic edge cases—they are the ordinary state of scientific inquiry, where several theories typically survive criticism simultaneously. The target thus overstates its conclusion: rather than dissolving the dilemma, it merely handles the degenerate single-survivor case while deferring the dilemma unchanged to the multi-survivor case. A claim that 'the underlying structure was never relevant' is directly contradicted by the target's own admission that it becomes relevant whenever a choice among unrefuted theories is required.
